While you won't usually find test points in consumer electronics they are usually prevalent in commercial and military electronics to speed the troubleshooting process and reduce the equipment down time.
Located between the output of the FM Detector and the input to the Audio Amplifier circuits is TP2 and at the output of IC U2 is TP3, test points to assist in the isolation of the fault.
IC U1 contains the IF Amplifier, Limiter, and the FM Detector. IC U2 is the Audio Amplifier. So, the next step is to further isolate the fault to one of these two ICs.

Studying the schematic shows that all the suspected circuits are located on the PC130-443 card. Further study shows the suspected circuits are incorporated in two IC's, U1 and U2, with some associated components.
Assuming the IF Amplifier is working makes the Limiter circuit, the FM Detector circuit, or the Audio Amplifier as the most likely suspect circuits causing the fault.

The FM receiver may detect noise or interference in the 88 -
108 MHz band. The station detector may detect non-FM signals. If the station detector needs adjustment, set to the level you want. There is no factory standard.
As you learned earlier in this lesson, the initial assessment phase of troubleshooting is vital. The more symptoms you discover, the more focused you can make your troubleshooting efforts.

Another factor that will affect any measurements of frequency is the limited ability of most average test equipment to measure frequencies as high and/or as weak as those found in the front end of FM receivers.
Bear in mind that, other than the clock and IF frequencies, the frequencies found in troubleshooting will be based upon the tuned frequency or the broadcast signal. station or a signal generator.

It should be remembered that some of the DC levels will vary, based upon the position of variable components in the receiver's circuits. You may want to take a few readings on a fully operational FM receiver and record the indications. This will be valuable data for troubleshooting.

If we remove power to the PC130-443 card and remove U1, a continuity check between pin 6 and TP2 reveals a reading of approximately 100 kW, the value of R9.
We've already determined that R9 is good, therefore, the problem must be either the run between R9 and pin 6, or, the Muting Network or Quadrature detector.
Since pin 7 is not used by the PC130-443 card, the signal must leave U1 through the Muting Network at pin 6. When we look for the signal at TP2, it is not present.

The presence of the signal at TP1 tells us that the limiter is working. Looking at the schematic of U1, the Limiter also outputs to the Quadrature Detector which outputs at pin 7 and internally to the Muting Network.
The Limiter outputs at pin 9 and also internally to the Quadrature Detector (discriminator). Using the oscilloscope, check for the signal at TP1.

The problem must therefore reside somewhere between TP2 and U1. We know that the signal is entering U1 and being processed as far as the Signal Strength Driver, which outputs to pin 5 and internally to the limiter.

The seasoned troubleshooter knows that all of these factors come into play when trying to solve a problem. It will not come as a shock to him or her that a suspect component is not the culprit at all.
Compounding this problem, our decisions and actions that follow are often based on those perceptions. It must be assumed then, that how we see something is at least as important as how it really is.

Because all of us think differently, how we perceive something might be radically in opposition to how the same thing is perceived by someone else. All the while, the perceptions of both may be false.
It is for this reason that the creative side of the brain must also be heavily engaged. The best troubleshooters are those that are able to exercise both modes of thought.

Because electronics is based on mathematics, using the logical side of the brain for troubleshooting is imperative. At the same time, a particular symptom may be caused by any number of reasons, many of which will not seem logical at all.
Troubleshooting is a process that involves theoretical knowledge, test equipment competency, and understanding the equipment operation, all blended together with a little bit of intuition.
